processing_steps.method: air induction melting with flux cover (AIMFC)
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Forty-kilogram melts of the five carbon-series alloys (Table IV) prepared by air induction melting with a flux cover (Al2O3, CaO, MgO, CaF2). Note: Table V and Fig. 5 captions label the carbon-series route 'AIM', while the section text states air induction melting with a flux cover.
Hot-forged in a 1-tonne pneumatic forge hammer with die platens at room temperature.
Hot rolled 50% with 1-mm reduction per pass; reheated after every six passes; final plate thickness 12 mm.

precipitates.distribution: fine dark speckles inside grains; grain boundaries largely clean

structures.overall_structure: Equiaxed grains with fine dark speckles (Fe3AlC0.5 precipitates) inside the grains; grain boundaries largely clean.

unmapped_findings: Measured composition (Table IV): Al 6.92, Si 0.17, Mn 0.18, S 0.005, C 0.15 wt.% [b0051,b0052].
The volume fraction of Fe3AlC0.5 precipitates increases significantly with increasing carbon content [b0061].
The increase in bulk hardness with carbon suggests precipitation hardening by hard Fe3AlC0.5 is the predominant strengthening mechanism [b0062].

Text b0062 states carbon addition to Fe-7 wt.% Al improved room-temperature strength (396–610 MPa) and decreased room-temperature tensile elongation (18–3%); these text ranges do not exactly match Table V values.
Conclusion (b0064): increasing carbon in Fe-7 wt.% Al significantly improves strength but adversely affects ductility.
